actions.reason: BasicTokenizer.encode used to rescan the whole id list for the lowest-index pair before every merge. Suppose every merge creates a token id larger than both of its children, and the merge ids are distinct. Then the lowest-index pair present is always the next merge in index order. A merge only creates new pairs that contain the new token, and those pairs have higher indices. So encode now checks that condition once per call. If it holds, encode works on a str with one character per token id (the bytes decoded as latin-1) and goes through the merges in index order. For each merge it does a substring test and, if the pair is found, one str.replace, which is the same left-to-right non-overlapping replacement as before. If the condition fails, the original loop runs. Outputs are identical. Measured encode_ir ratio 0.4330. Other metrics are within noise.

@@ -124,6 +124,26 @@ class BasicTokenizer(Tokenizer):
     def encode(self, text):
         # given a string text, return the token ids
         text_bytes = text.encode("utf-8") # raw bytes
+        # when every merge creates a token id larger than both of its children
+        # (and ids are distinct), the lowest-index pair present is always the
+        # next merge in index order, so the merges can be applied in that order
+        # on a str holding one character per token id
+        ordered = sorted(self.merges.items(), key=lambda item: item[1])
+        prev = -1
+        for (p0, p1), idx in ordered:
+            if not (type(p0) is int and type(p1) is int and type(idx) is int
+                    and 0 <= p0 < idx and 0 <= p1 < idx and prev < idx < 0x110000):
+                break
+            prev = idx
+        else:
+            s = text_bytes.decode("latin-1")
+            for (p0, p1), idx in ordered:
+                if len(s) < 2:
+                    break
+                pair = chr(p0) + chr(p1)
+                if pair in s:
+                    s = s.replace(pair, chr(idx))
+            return [ord(c) for c in s]
         ids = list(text_bytes) # list of integers in range 0..255
         merge_map = build_merge_map(self.merges)
         while len(ids) >= 2:

journal.text:
I changed BasicTokenizer.encode in minbpe/basic.py, lines 127-128, replacing 2 lines with 22. The old loop rescanned the whole id list for the lowest-index pair before every merge. If every merge creates an id larger than both children and merge ids are distinct, the lowest-index pair present is always the next merge in index order. A merge only creates pairs containing the new token, and those have higher indices. So encode now walks the merges in order.

My sandbox evaluation accepted it with identical outputs. encode_ir went from 1844887567 to 798908769, ratio 0.4330. train_basic_ir was 1.0015, train_regex_ir 1.0007, decode_ir 1.0010 and save_load_ir 1.0025. All guards were within limits. This is not a verdict. Replays decide.

I believe encode correctness rests on that id-ordering assumption, which minbpe training satisfies. Loaded merges that break it would be wrong.

Next I will check RegexTokenizer encode in minbpe/regex.py for the same pattern. I will also check whether the assumption needs a guard on load.
